newsitem.title: USA: White House counsel will testify on documents.
newsitem.headline: White House counsel will testify on documents.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent

White House counsel Charles Ruff agreed on Wednesday to testify to a House of Representatives committee investigating campaign fund-raising misdeeds in a potentially explosive hearing rescheduled for next week.

Facing the threat of criminal "contempt of Congress" charges, Ruff agreed to appear before the House government reform and oversight committee on Thursday to explain why he refused to hand over sensitive fund-raising documents.
But the committee chairman, Indiana Republican Dan Burton, said he would give Ruff extra time to prepare by delaying the hearing until next Wednesday.
"Mr. Ruff says he needs more time to prepare a response. This should satisfy his need," he said.

The committee was investigating whether China and other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by helping President Bill Clinton and the Democratic Party with illegal political contributions.

They also were investigating whether the White House or the Democrats knowingly solicited, received or laundered foreign funds. The FBI and a Senate committee were conducting simultaneous but separate investigations.
Ruff was summoned to explain why the White House has refused to comply with subpoenas of documents relating to possible illegal campaign contributions by foreigners.

Burton, in a letter to Ruff on Wednesday, demanded that he make good on a promise to deliver a list of the documents over which Clinton is claiming the privilege of confidentiality between attorney and client. Ruff had promised to provide the log by Tuesday but failed to do so.
The hearing loomed as the next flashpoint in a growing confrontation between Republicans and the White House.
If Ruff refuses to hand over the documents, the committee could vote on a "contempt of Congress" resolution. Ruff would then have to comply, or take the matter to court to avoid criminal sanctions.
In a letter to Ruff last Friday, Burton said the White House had been stonewalling for months.
"Given the White House response to date, I have concluded ... that I have no alternative but to hold a hearing to consider your refusal to fully respond to the committee's subpoenas," Burton wrote.
"I am formally requesting that you attend to explain why you should not be held in contempt of Congress," he added.

The White House has said it would allow Burton and his investigators to look at the documents it wants to see but not to copy or remove them from the White House because of the danger they would be leaked to the media.
Some of the documents relate to former Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell, who was recently released after serving a jail sentence for defrauding his Arkansas law firm.
In the period between resigning from the Justice Department and beginning his sentence, Hubbell received more than $500,000 from various individuals and companies for work as a legal consultant.
Burton suspects it was hush money to prevent him testifying about what he knew. Hubbell indicated he will invoke the Fifth Amendment and refuse to testify further.

Other documents demanded by the committee related to the activities of Asian-Americans and Asian business interests, including former Democratic fund-raiser John Huang. Burton has said he suspects Huang was a spy working for China.
